evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with atopic dermatitis: clinical diagnosis, severity scoring, stepwise therapy from emollients and topical agents to systemic therapy, comorbidities, referral and pregnancy considerations. Verified against the Saudi Ministry of Health national guideline (V2.2, 2021) and FDA labels.
findings: The Saudi Ministry of Health national AD guideline (V2.2, June 2021) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, including Figure 2 and Table 2 as images; page locators are the printed page numbers.
The guideline is consensus-based (75% agreement threshold) and does not grade recommendation strength (printed p. 6).
Contraindications come from US FDA labels read via openFDA on 13 Oct 2026; several labels are for other indications.
unverifiedSections: SFDA register not checked directly; SFDA approval statements are those printed in the 2021 Saudi MoH guideline and may have changed
No international AD guideline (AAD, EADV, NICE adult) was opened; NICE CG57 covers children under 12 only
JAK inhibitor doses, boxed warnings and contraindications not reproduced
Doses of topical corticosteroids by potency class and amounts are not given in the Saudi guideline
The EASI 51 eligibility threshold is printed as '51 or more' with a '51.1 to 72 very severe' band; reproduced as printed
FDA labels are US labels; Saudi product information may differ

pathophysiology.summary: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with intense itching and recurrent eczematous lesions. The Saudi Ministry of Health guideline covers adults and children; this topic covers adults only. Management is stepwise from emollients and topical anti-inflammatories, through phototherapy, to systemic therapy chosen by severity scores.
keyMechanisms: Pathogenesis combines genetic susceptibility, skin barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation (MoH AD guideline printed p. 5).
Impaired skin barrier function, including moisturising factors, allows allergens in and triggers flares; moisturisers suppress itch and help maintain barrier function (printed p. 11).
Barrier disruption increases absorption of irritants and allergens, which leads to immune activation and contact sensitisation, so allergic contact dermatitis may be more common in AD (printed p. 9).

Infection risk is raised through immune dysregulation, barrier dysfunction, lower antimicrobial peptides and bacterial colonisation; 70% of patients are colonised with Staphylococcus aureus on lesional skin (printed pp. 9–10).
Intense itch, sleep disturbance, stigma and neuro-inflammation are postulated to contribute to anxiety, depression, suicidality and ADHD in AD (printed p. 9).

references.title: National Saudi Guidelines for the Management of Atopic Dermatitis (Saudi Ministry of Health)
references.edition: Version 2.2, June 2021 (consensus meetings January to March 2021), printed pp. 5, 9–11

symptoms: Intense itching (pruritus) is an essential diagnostic feature (MoH AD guideline printed pp. 5 and 25, Table 1).
Recurrent eczematous lesions with a chronic or relapsing history (printed pp. 5 and 25, Table 1).
In adults the flexural surfaces of the extremities are frequently affected (printed p. 5).
Sleep disturbance and impaired quality of life accompany severe disease (printed p. 9).
physicalSigns: Eczema, acute, subacute or chronic, with typical morphology and age-specific pattern; current or previous flexural lesions at any age; sparing of the groin and axillary regions (printed p. 25, Table 1).

Supporting features: xerosis, keratosis pilaris, pityriasis alba, hyperlinear palms, ichthyosis, periorbital changes, perioral and periauricular lesions, perifollicular accentuation, lichenification and prurigo lesions (printed p. 25, Table 1).
Atypical vascular responses such as facial pallor, white dermographism and delayed blanch response are associated but non-specific (printed p. 25, Table 1).
redFlags: Suspected eczema herpeticum: urgent dermatology referral, ideally within 1 to 2 weeks (printed p. 18). Severe disease correlates strongly with eczema herpeticum (printed p. 9).
Clinically infected skin: systemic antibiotics are for clinical infection, not for a positive S. aureus culture alone (printed p. 9).
A history of recurrent infections may suggest an underlying immune deficiency (printed p. 10).
Severe AD unresponsive to optimal topical therapy at 2 to 4 weeks, or failed treatment of bacterial infection: refer to a dermatologist (printed p. 18).
Recent onset or worsening with limited response to treatment or atypical distribution: consider contact allergy (printed p. 13).
precipitants: Non-specific irritation: sweat, saliva, hair, friction from clothes, rough textured clothing such as wool, and scratching (printed pp. 12–13).
Contact allergens in cosmetics, perfumes, metals, topical drugs, plants and skin or hair care products (printed p. 13).
Food allergens; in older children and adults pollen-related food allergens are mostly associated with exacerbations (printed p. 13).
Aeroallergens: mites, house dust, pollen and pet hair (printed p. 13).
Prolonged showers and hot water; the guideline advises 37 to 38 °C (printed p. 12).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: AAD diagnostic criteria: essential features (MoH AD guideline printed pp. 7 and 25, Table 1)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Pruritus must be present, and eczema (acute, subacute or chronic) with a chronic or relapsing history, typical morphology and age-specific pattern, current or previous flexural lesions at any age, and sparing of the groin and axillary regions
Early age of onset; atopy (personal or family history, IgE reactivity); xerosis. Seen in most cases and supportive

Diagnosis depends on excluding scabies, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, ichthyosis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, psoriasis, photosensitivity dermatoses, immune deficiency diseases and erythroderma of other causes

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Severity tools recommended for use in clinic (printed p. 7)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: PGA, EASI, pruritus NRS and DLQI; EASI is required for Saudi MoH regulatory and payer reimbursement purposes

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Criteria for systemic therapy (printed p. 24, Figure 2)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: EASI 16 or more, DLQI 10 or more, pruritus NRS 4 or more, PGA 3 or more, or BSA 10% or more; flare recurrence, persistence and disease site are also considered

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Eligibility for anti-JAK or biologic therapy at Saudi MoH, as third line (printed p. 10)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Any one of: EASI 51 or more (as printed); DLQI 21 or more; pruritus NRS 7 or more; PGA 5 or more; BSA 20% or more
Both: EASI 75 response, and NRS below 4 or DLQI 5 or less

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Treatment failure of first-line therapy (printed p. 18)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Inadequate response after 4 to 8 weeks of appropriate topical therapy, with or without 12 to 16 weeks of phototherapy

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Stopping dupilumab or anti-JAK therapy (printed p. 18)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Stop at 16 weeks if there is no adequate response: EASI reduced by less than 50%, or DLQI improved by less than 4 points from baseline

ruleIn.testName: Clinical diagnosis using the American Academy of Dermatology criteria
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Pruritus plus eczema with chronic or relapsing course, typical morphology and distribution, flexural involvement and sparing of the groin and axillae, with supporting atopy, early onset and xerosis.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: AD is a clinical diagnosis based on morphology, age-dependent distribution and associated signs; the guideline recommends the AAD criteria for a definite diagnosis (printed pp. 7 and 25).
ruleIn.normalValue: No serological marker exists; the guideline gives no laboratory normal value

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess severity and triggers
actions: Diagnose clinically with the AAD criteria and exclude the conditions listed in Table 1 (printed pp. 7 and 25).
Record EASI, PGA, pruritus NRS and DLQI at baseline; EASI is required for Saudi MoH reimbursement (printed p. 7).
Set treatment goals with the patient before starting (printed p. 11).

Look for comorbidities: asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, eosinophilic oesophagitis, allergic contact dermatitis, anxiety and depression, infections, and cardio-metabolic risk (printed pp. 8–10).

clinicalManagement.title: Education, emollients and trigger avoidance
actions: Apply liberal amounts of emollient twice daily and after bathing (soak and seal) and continue after remission (printed pp. 11–12).
Choose emollients with the fewest ingredients and avoid fragrances and preservatives; avoid products with peanut, oat or wheat proteins in children under 2 years (printed p. 11).
Cleanse with low-irritant, non-allergenic products, avoid prolonged showers, and keep water at 37 to 38 °C (printed p. 12).
Consider intermittent antiseptic baths in recurrent skin infections, for example one quarter to one half cup of 6% household bleach in a full bathtub of about 40 gallons (printed p. 12).
Teach avoidance of irritants and scratching: wipe away sweat and saliva, avoid wool, keep nails short, wear long sleeves and trousers (printed pp. 12–13).

clinicalManagement.title: First-line anti-inflammatory therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 4 to 8 weeks of topical therapy; 12 to 16 weeks of phototherapy
actions: Topical corticosteroid is the mainstay and first-line anti-inflammatory treatment; apply twice daily, tailoring potency and vehicle to age, site, severity and duration (printed p. 14).

Flares are safe to treat for up to 4 weeks, and many settle with 1 to 2 weeks; for maintenance use a topical corticosteroid proactively, for example twice weekly, with emollient for up to 16 weeks (printed p. 14).
Very potent (class I) corticosteroids are not recommended for AD (printed p. 14). Monitor long-term users by regular examination for skin side effects (printed p. 14).

Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are second-line, and can be used off label first-line in sensitive areas and for long-term therapy; they can be combined with a topical corticosteroid. Proactive tacrolimus twice weekly for up to 52 weeks reduces flares (printed pp. 14–15).
Crisaborole (PDE4 inhibitor) is indicated for mild-to-moderate AD but is not SFDA registered (printed pp. 15 and 27).
Phototherapy (NB-UVB or UVA1) is an acceptable add-on for moderate-to-severe AD where available, or monotherapy when topical anti-inflammatories are unsuitable (printed pp. 15–16).

branches.condition: Response achieved (EASI 75 and NRS below 4 or DLQI 5 or less by 16 weeks)
actions: Continue treatment, with continued emollient use (printed pp. 11 and 24).

branches.condition: Treatment goal not achieved after 4 to 8 weeks of topical therapy (with or without 12 to 16 weeks of phototherapy)
actions: Move to systemic therapy if criteria are met: EASI 16 or more, DLQI 10 or more, NRS 4 or more, PGA 3 or more or BSA 10% or more (printed pp. 18 and 24).

clinicalManagement.title: Second-line: conventional systemic therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Reassess at 6 weeks for cyclosporine, 12 weeks for others
actions: Options are cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil; the guideline does not prefer one over another, and cost and safety are weighed (printed pp. 16, 18 and 24).
Use short courses of systemic corticosteroid only for acute exacerbations; avoid long-term use and consider flare-up on stopping (printed p. 16).
Do baseline and follow-up monitoring as in the Table 4 monitoring table (printed pp. 29–30).
Evaluate response after 12 weeks, or 6 weeks for cyclosporine; if no improvement, optimise the dose or switch (printed p. 18).

clinicalManagement.title: Third-line: dupilumab or JAK inhibitor
actions: Offer dupilumab or an anti-JAK agent to those meeting the Saudi MoH criteria: EASI 51 or more (as printed), DLQI 21 or more, NRS 7 or more, PGA 5 or more or BSA 20% or more (printed p. 10).

Dupilumab is SFDA approved for moderate-to-severe AD not optimally responsive to topical therapy or after failure of one or more oral immunosuppressants; combine with daily emollient and topical anti-inflammatories as needed (printed pp. 16–17).

Baricitinib and upadacitinib are SFDA approved for moderate-to-severe AD in adults who are candidates for systemic therapy; abrocitinib is approved for adults only per the guideline; tralokinumab is not yet SFDA approved (printed p. 17).
Stop dupilumab or the JAK inhibitor at 16 weeks if there is no adequate response (EASI reduction below 50%, DLQI improvement below 4 points) (printed p. 18).

clinicalManagement.title: Fourth-line and referral
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When third-line fails or red flags appear
actions: Optimise the dose or combine with conventional systemic therapy with or without phototherapy, considering cost and safety (printed p. 24, Figure 2).
Reconsider the diagnosis in refractory cases (printed p. 18).

Same-day or urgent referral for suspected eczema herpeticum (printed p. 18). Routine referral (seen within 1 to 4 weeks ideally) if the diagnosis is uncertain, response is partial, the face, genitalia, palms or soles are affected, infections are severe and recurrent, contact allergy is suspected, quality of life is poor, or food allergy is suspected (printed pp. 18–19).

regimens.duration: Up to 4 weeks for a flare; 1 to 2 weeks often enough; proactive maintenance, for example twice weekly, up to 16 weeks
adjustments: Tailor potency and vehicle to age, body area, severity and duration
Class I very potent corticosteroids are not recommended for AD
Pregnancy and lactation: topical corticosteroids are first-line and considered safe; striae risk with potent steroids on the abdomen and thighs (printed pp. 14 and 20)
monitoring: Regular physical examination for cutaneous side effects in long-term users (printed p. 14)

learningObjectives: Diagnose AD clinically using the AAD criteria and exclude mimics.
Measure severity with EASI, PGA, NRS and DLQI and set treatment goals.
Apply the stepwise treatment ladder and know referral triggers.
keyPoints: AD is a clinical diagnosis: pruritus plus eczema with chronic or relapsing course and typical distribution.
Emollients twice daily and after bathing are the base of treatment; topical corticosteroids are first-line.
Treatment goal within 16 weeks: EASI 75 and NRS below 4 or DLQI 5 or less.
Stop dupilumab or JAK inhibitor at 16 weeks without adequate response.
pitfalls: Treating a positive S. aureus culture with systemic antibiotics when the skin is not clinically infected (printed p. 9).
Using very potent class I corticosteroids for AD (printed p. 14).
Eliminating foods without clear evidence of food allergy (printed p. 13).
Missing eczema herpeticum: refer urgently (printed p. 18).
Using methotrexate or mycophenolate in pregnancy: contraindicated (printed p. 21).

references.locator: Printed pp. 5–21 (sections 1 to 5), p. 24 (Figure 2), p. 25 (Table 1), p. 26 (Table 2), p. 27 (Table 3), pp. 28–34 (Tables 4 and 5)

patientEducation: Education improves adherence, outcomes and quality of life; teach emollients, cleansing and trigger avoidance (printed pp. 11–13).
Explain that scratching and irritants worsen flares, and how to keep nails short and use suitable clothing (printed pp. 12–13).
Explain that long-term systemic steroids are avoided (printed p. 16).

Women planning pregnancy: topical corticosteroids are first-line in pregnancy and lactation; phototherapy is safe, and folic acid should be considered; methotrexate and mycophenolate are contraindicated, and the decision on systemic therapy involves obstetricians (printed pp. 20–21).
lifestyleAndDiet: Limit shower time and keep water at 37 to 38 °C; showering daily or twice weekly made no difference if skin hydration is maintained (printed p. 12).
Do not eliminate foods without clear evidence of food allergy (printed p. 13).
AD is associated with higher cardio-metabolic risk; the guideline lists sleep disturbance, sedentary lifestyle, obesity and smoking as contributors (printed p. 10).
mdtReferrals: Dermatologist: urgent for suspected eczema herpeticum; routine for uncertain diagnosis, partial response, face, genital, palm or sole disease, recurrent infection, suspected contact allergy (printed pp. 18–19).
Allergist-immunologist for suspected food allergy; specialist investigation for moderate or severe AD with suspected food allergy (printed pp. 13 and 19).
Psychological advice if AD is controlled but quality of life or psychological wellbeing remain poor (printed p. 19).
dischargeCriteria: Treatment goal reached: EASI 75 response and NRS below 4 or DLQI 5 or less (printed p. 11).
Patient taught emollient use, trigger avoidance and when to seek help (printed pp. 11–13).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Reassess against the treatment goals at 4 to 8 weeks on topical therapy, 12 weeks on systemic therapy (6 weeks on cyclosporine), and 16 weeks on dupilumab or a JAK inhibitor (printed pp. 11, 18 and 24). Long-term topical corticosteroid users need regular examination for skin side effects (printed p. 14). Vaccination, including varicella, is recommended; AD is not a contraindication to vaccination (printed p. 21).
